extracted.intended_audience: first-year undergraduate mathematics students (learners of proof techniques)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for constructing and presenting rigorous proofs in undergraduate pure mathematics, covering methods (induction, contradiction, contrapositive), common pitfalls, presentation tips, and elementary set-theory proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Mathematical Induction (base/hypothesis/step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let P(n) be statements for n ∈ N. Suppose (i) P(1) is true, and (ii) P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) for all k ∈ N. Then P(n) is true for all n ∈ N. When constructing an induction proof present P(n) and follow three steps: INDUCTION BASE (check P(1)), INDUCTION HYPOTHESIS (assume P(k)), INDUCTION STEP (show P(k) ⇒ P(k+1)), finish with conclusion invoking the Principle of Mathematical Induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit labels 'BASE', 'INDUCTION HYPOTHESIS', 'INDUCTION STEP' and conclude e.g. 'since P(1) is true and P(k) ⇒ P(k+1), P(n) holds by the Principle of Mathematical Induction'. The 'dominoes effect' analogy is useful. Be careful that the induction hypothesis is an assumption to be used, not an already proved fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong Mathematical Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Variant: Let P(n) be statements with r ≤ k. Suppose (i) P(r) is true, and (ii) P(j) ⇒ P(k+1) for all r ≤ j ≤ k. Then P(n) is true for all n ≥ r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when P(k+1) requires multiple earlier cases (not only P(k)). State base at r and the stronger hypothesis (assume P(r), P(r+1),...,P(k)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing the induction base (start at r)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the statement fails for the first few n, change the base step: check P(r) is true for some r ∈ N and continue induction for n ≥ r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the starting index explicit in both base checks and final conclusion (e.g., conclude 'for all n ≥ r'). Ensure you check all necessary initial cases (e.g., if the induction step uses P(k) and P(k−1), you must check P(r) and P(r+1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using multiple assumptions in the induction hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes proving P(k+1) requires assuming more than one previous case (e.g., P(k) and P(k−1)), so include those in the hypothesis and ensure the base covers the needed initial cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you assume P(1) and P(2) you must check both in the base. State clearly which previous cases are assumed in the induction hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture variant of induction (combined start and multiple assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start the induction base at some r ∈ N and show that P(r), P(r+1), ..., P(k) imply P(k+1). Then conclude P(n) for all n ≥ r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the list of assumed cases and the range for k; verify all initial cases up to the first k used in the step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction common pitfalls and hard parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Common difficulties: the induction hypothesis appears as 'assuming what needs to be proved'; it's easy to get confused and make the inductive step wrong (example of a fallacious induction exists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully check where the inductive step uses the hypothesis; ensure no unjustified jumps. When a proof seems to 'have all parts' (base, hypothesis, step) verify each step rigorously (e.g., ensure correct domain like n ≥ 2 is stated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure for an induction proof (presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing induction proofs, explicitly state P(n), present BASE, INDUCTION HYPOTHESIS, INDUCTION STEP, then a concluding sentence invoking the Principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label the parts, show intermediate algebraic manipulations (as in examples), and conclude with the domain ('for all n' or 'for all n ≥ r'). Avoid skipping algebraic steps (show multiplication, subtraction, rearrangement where used).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A ⇒ B by contradiction: assume A and not B and derive a contradiction. Often used for existence/nonexistence statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finish with an explicit 'contradiction!' or symbol. Be careful that contradictions arise from the assumption, not from an error in the middle of the argument. When definitions are central (rational/irrational), use them to express assumed negation concretely (e.g., express supposed rational as p/q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction: hard parts / pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving complex theorems it is easy to make mistakes that create contradictions coming from errors, not the original assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track each logical step to ensure the contradiction truly follows from the assumed negation. Use precise definitions to avoid ambiguous intermediate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contrapositive (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A ⇒ B, show the equivalent statement not B ⇒ not A. The contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is effective when direct proof is awkward. Use concrete assumptions for 'not B' and deduce 'not A'. The Wason selection task illustrates testing implications by checking appropriate cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and use definitions correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: A major source of error is misunderstanding definitions. Know definitions (e.g., rational/irrational, injective/surjective, subset) and use them precisely in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecturers expect accurate use of definitions. If you don't know the definition of the object you work with, you won't know where to start. When in doubt, restate the definition in words before using it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write enough words (explain steps in prose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not prioritise symbols over words; include explanatory phrases and sentences so the argument is easy to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At least for early undergraduate work, use words to explain why one statement implies another (e.g., 'because', 'therefore', 'hence'). Prefer short explanatory phrases: '(statement B) follows from (statement A) because...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure you understand every line (no rote memorisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand every line you write; avoid memorising proofs without comprehension. Gaps where the student cannot proceed indicate lack of understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can reverse or reconstruct steps, you likely understand them. Practice by writing proofs and explaining each step in your own words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incorrect steps and unjustified leaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'jump' to a required form without showing the intermediate reasoning; missing lines are penalised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the reasoning that leads to algebraic rearrangements or logical deductions; if a highlighted step is missing, the argument is incomplete. Provide the minimal but sufficient intermediate steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layout and presentation matter
rubrics_metrics.description: How you lay out a proof is at least as important as the content. A correct argument must be presented clearly (not 'it's all in there somewhere').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by outlining assumptions and the goal, label parts of proof, use full punctuation and correct English, include brief explanatory phrases, and remove rough work in the final version while keeping all logical steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: State domains and explicit conclusion ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the domain/indices in your statement and conclusion (e.g., if a proof only holds for n ≥ 2, state that in the conclusion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When induction starts at r or when an argument only works from a particular index, include 'for all n ≥ r' in the concluding sentence; check the appropriate base cases accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-proof technique: proving subset and equality
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A ⊆ B, choose an arbitrary element x ∈ A and prove x ∈ B. To show A = B, prove both A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'let x be arbitrary in A' and follow implications. For proper subset A ⊂ B show A ⊆ B and provide an element of B not in A. Often use element-chasing with explicit membership proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe sets and domains unambiguously
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing a set use clear set-builder notation with the domain specified (e.g., {x ∈ R : 2 < x < 3}), otherwise expressions like '{2 < x < 3}' are meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always specify the universe (R, N, Z, etc.) for variables in set descriptions. For intervals use standard notation [a,b), (a,∞), etc., and remember ∞ is not a real number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality: finite vs infinite sets
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite sets |A| is the number of elements. For infinite sets define 'same cardinality' via existence of a bijection between sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate |A| = |B| (numeric equality of cardinalities) with A = B (same elements). For infinite sets argue by constructing or referencing bijections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standard set operations and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use correct definitions of union, intersection, relative complement, complement (with universal set specified), and Cartesian product in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}, A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}, A\B = {x ∈ A : x ∉ B}, Ac = {x : x ∉ A} where U (universal set) is specified; A × B = {(a,b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}. Use these definitions when proving set identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common pedagogical advice for developing proof skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice many proofs, study lecture proofs as models, experiment with different methods, and ask for feedback; writing proofs takes time and iterative polishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through rough drafts, create your own examples, and be prepared to rewrite the final version cleanly. Try reversing the argument or working from both ends to find a pathway, but present the final proof in forward logical order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common mistakes summary (what markers look for)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent student errors: misunderstanding definitions, insufficient words/explanations, lack of understanding of steps, incorrect or omitted logical steps, misuse of induction or contradiction, and attempting to memorise proofs rather than understand them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markers expect clear definitions, textual explanations for symbol-heavy arguments, correctly justified steps, correct base cases in induction, and explicit statement of ranges/domains. Treat mistakes as learning steps; seek practice and feedback.
